text:
The screen door at the back of my mother’s house in Mercer had lost its hydraulic hiss sometime during the first term of the Obama Administration, and so my arrival was announced, as it had been for the past fifteen years, by a sharp, wooden slap that rattled the glass panes of the mudroom.

“Don’t let the flies in,” she called from the kitchen, though it was only late May and the flies had not yet arrived in any meaningful constituency.

“I’m already in,” I said, setting my canvas overnight bag on the linoleum beside her clay-caked gardening clogs. 

She was standing at the sink, paring the bruised quarters from a hill of McIntosh apples she had kept in the root cellar since November. They were wrinkled and soft as baseballs left out in the rain, their skins slipping beneath the thumb-worn blade of her paring knife, which had been sharpened over forty years into a crescent needle. My mother, at eighty-two, had undergone a similar whittling. Each time I drove the three hours north from the city, she seemed to have ceded another half-inch to gravity, her collarbone more avian under her boat-necked cotton shirts, her silver hair finer against the window light.

“You took the Taconic,” she said. It was not a question. She held a profound, lifelong distrust of the Taconic State Parkway, which she believed was engineered exclusively for roadsters driven by reckless men in wool caps.

“I took the Thruway,” I lied, kissing the dry, powdery depression of her cheek. She smelled of Pond’s cold cream, crushed mint, and the faintly metallic scent of the well water. “Traffic was nothing.”

“Well,” she said skeptically, dropping a ribbon of peel into a ceramic bowl. “Take those tomatoes off the windowsill and see if any are soft enough for sandwiches. The bread is in the breadbox, though why I bought a whole loaf when I’m only one person is a mystery for the ages.”

This was the grammar of our visits: a series of minor, rhythmic corrections followed immediately by the distribution of domestic labor. Within ten minutes of walking through the door, I was no longer a forty-eight-year-old copy editor with a bad lower back and an ex-wife in Brooklyn; I was simply the tallest person in the house, useful for reaching the ironstone platter on the top shelf and loosening the lids on jars of piccalilli that had fused shut in the basement dark.

We ate on the screened porch, which faced a sloping half-acre of untamed timothy grass and the stone foundation of a barn that had burned down before my father bought the property in 1968. 

“The Miller girl bought the old pharmacy,” she told me, cutting her sandwich into quarters with surgical precision. “Turned it into a place that sells candles that smell like dirt. Fourteen dollars for a jar of wax the size of a teacup. I went in there last Tuesday just to see if she’d kept old Mr. Gable’s apothecary drawers, and she had them painted white. Chalk paint, she called it. Looked like somebody spilled milk of magnesia all over good cherrywood.”

“Which Miller girl?” I asked. “Sarah?”

“The younger one. With the teeth.”

“Hannah,” I said, retrieving from some deep sedimentary layer of memory a girl who had worn headgear to the seventh-grade cotillion. “She must be forty-five now, Mom.”

“Well, she still has the teeth,” my mother said, not unkindly. “And no sense about cherrywood.”

After lunch, I offered to clear the gutters or take the brush hog to the weeds encroaching on the lilac bushes, chores my father would have completed by mid-April before his heart gave out in the aisle of the Agway twelve years ago. My mother waved the offer away.

“The man comes on Thursdays for the grass,” she said. “Though he charges me forty dollars just to ride around on that noisy tractor like he’s King Farouk. What I really need is for us to go down to the nursery on Route 9 and get the flats. If I don’t get the marigolds in around the lettuce before the June bugs hatch, I might as well just set a salad bowl out in the yard for the rabbits.”

We took my car, which she complained rode too low to the asphalt. At the nursery, a sprawling affair of hoop houses and gravel paths that radiated a wet, vegetative heat under the May sun, my mother moved with a terrifying, single-minded briskness. I followed behind her with a rusted red flatbed wagon, watching the crown of her straw sun hat bob among the hanging baskets of fuchsias. 

“Put two of the lemon verbena in the back,” she instructed, pointing with an unpaid-for trowel. “And six of the Sungolds. Not the ones on the end—they’ve been leggy since last week. Get the ones from the back tray where the hose reaches.”

“You don’t eat six plants’ worth of cherry tomatoes, Mom,” I said, lifting the damp black plastic flats onto the wagon. “Last August you had them lined up on every windowsill in the dining room like billiard balls.”

“Mrs. Gable takes them,” she said, already moving toward the perennials. “And I like to look at them. A house without something ripening in it is just a waiting room.”

When we returned home, the sun had shifted west, throwing long, bruised shadows across the driveway. The air had turned heavy, hinting at the unseasonable humidity predicted for the week. I carried the flats around to the kitchen garden behind the garage, a neat rectangle fenced in with chicken wire patched with green twine. 

I wanted her to sit in the aluminum lawn chair in the shade while I dug the holes, capability being the only currency I knew how to spend in her presence, but she insisted on kneeling beside me on her green foam pad. For an hour, we worked in a companionable silence, the only sounds the scrape of my spade against buried shale and the dry *snip* of her shears.

“Your father never liked Sungolds,” she remarked, tamping the dark soil around a slender green stalk. “He said a tomato ought to be red and big enough to cover a piece of toast. He had very narrow ideas about vegetables. Do you remember that summer he tried to grow peanuts?”

“He read an article in *Popular Mechanics*,” I said, smiling at the dirt between my knees. “He thought he was George Washington Carver.”

“He got four peanuts,” she said, sitting back on her heels and wiping her forehead with her forearm, leaving a streak of gray silt above her eyebrow. “Four little gray nuts that tasted like boiled wool. He kept them in an empty Sucrets tin in his dresser until the day he died. I found them when I was clearing out his socks. I didn’t have the heart to throw them out, so I buried them out by the birdbath.”

I looked at her then—really looked at her, in that sudden, arresting way one sometimes sees a parent when the filter of familiarity drops away. The afternoon light caught the fine white hairs along her jawline and the deep creases above her lip. Her hands, resting in her lap, were a map of violet veins and swollen knuckles. A sharp, preemptive grief went through me, cold as well water.

“You shouldn’t be out here when it gets hot next week,” I said, my voice coming out rough. “They’re saying it’s going to hit ninety by Wednesday. Promise me you’ll leave the weeding until the evening.”

“I’ve lived through eighty-two summers, Paul,” she said, reaching for the marigolds. “I know what the sun feels like. Hand me the bone meal.”

Before I left that evening, she stood at the counter and assembled my care package—wrapping four slices of her meatloaf in aluminum foil with tight, hospital corners, and pouring a quart of cold brewed tea into an old mayonnaise jar. At the screen door, she reached up to pat my cheek, her palm dry and smelling of tomato leaf, that sharp, green perfume that stays on the skin even after soap.

“Call me when you get past the bridge,” she said. “So I know you didn’t hit a deer.”

“Nobody hits deer on the George Washington Bridge, Mom.”

“Well, if anybody could find one up there, it’d be you,” she said, and let the door slap shut between us.

***

The heat didn't break in June; it settled over the Northeast like a wet wool blanket. I spoke to my mother every Sunday and Wednesday evening. She reported that the Sungolds were waist-high, and that the well pump was making a noise like a cat with a hairball, though the plumber claimed to hear nothing at all.

The call came on a Tuesday afternoon in late June, from the landline of the retired guidance counselor who lived down the road. He had gone over to drop off some rhubarb and found her sitting on the bottom step of the back porch, her straw hat in her lap, speaking very politely in French—a language she had not studied since 1958—to a watering can.

By the time I fought my way up the Hudson, she was in a bed on the third floor of the county hospital in Poughkeepsie, tethered to an IV pole.

“Heat exhaustion,” the young resident told me in the hallway. “Bordering on stroke. Her core temp was a hundred and three when the ambulance brought her in, and her sodium was all over the map. At her age, the hypothalamus doesn't regulate thirst the way it used to. They don't know they're dehydrating until the confusion sets in.”

In the dim, chilled room, my mother looked terribly small against the industrial white of the hospital linens. When I pulled the vinyl armchair up to the rail of her bed and took her hand, her skin felt like dry parchment—hot, light, and fragile enough to tear.

“You took the Taconic,” she whispered, her eyes remaining closed.

“The Thruway, Mom,” I said, checking the glowing numbers on the IV machine. “I’m going to go back to the house tonight and get your nightgowns and your slippers. Is there anything else you want?”

She opened her eyes then, just a slit, her slate-blue irises milky under the fluorescent fixture. “The water,” she murmured, her brow furrowing with frantic concentration. “I left the water running on the lettuce. The well will go dry.”

“I’ll turn it off,” I promised. “Right when I get there. Don’t worry about the well.”

It was nearly nine o'clock when I turned into her driveway. The house was completely dark, something I had never seen before. Inside, the mudroom was stifling, thick with the baked smell of old pine boards. Without my mother’s small, corrective presence, the rooms felt vast and indifferent, the ticking of the hall clock intolerably loud. I went out the back door first, using the flashlight on my phone to keep my promise. 

The garden was a tangle of dark, humid life in the narrow white beam. The Sungolds had grown past the tops of their wire cages, weighted down with clusters of tiny green and orange spheres. The brass nozzle of the hose lay between two rows of wilted romaine, though the spigot at the garage had been turned off tightly—she had remembered to do it before sitting down on the steps, even as her mind was slipping back to high school French. 

When I went back inside to pack her bag, I found that the past month had barely registered on the interior of the house; or rather, that the day I had spent with her in May was still sitting out on the surfaces, preserved in the dry amber of her solitude. 

On the kitchen counter, tucked neatly behind the toaster, was the receipt from the nursery on Route 9, weighted down with a smooth river stone. Across the top, in her spidery cursive, she had written: *Paul’s visit—$34.60 (too much for verbena).* 

I opened the refrigerator. The shelves were nearly bare—a carton of eggs with three left, a tub of margarine, the jar of piccalilli I had opened for her four weeks ago. And there, on the middle shelf, covered in aluminum foil crimped with neat, hospital corners, was the other half of the meatloaf she had made for my lunch in May. She had wrapped it up the afternoon I left, slid it onto the wire rack, and simply forgotten to eat it, or perhaps had decided, in the economizing logic of her eighty-third year, that meatloaf was food for company, and she was back to toast and tea.

I stood in the center of the warm kitchen, the refrigerator door open against my hip, letting the cold air spill over my shoes. Through the screen door came the relentless, high-pitched trill of the tree frogs down by the burned-out barn, a sound that in my childhood had meant the summer was endless, a wide green sea you could swim in until September. 

The compressor kicked on with a shuddering sigh, working hard against the dark, heavy air of the house to keep the remnants of our lunch cold for a little while longer. I closed the refrigerator door, went upstairs to fetch her nightgown and her slippers, and came back down to lock the house up for the night, careful to catch the screen door with my heel so it wouldn't slap.
